summary: Peter Steinberger delivers a 'State of the Claw' keynote and subsequent audience Q&A moderated by Swyx. OpenClaw, at five months old, is the fastest-growing GitHub project with ~30,000 stars, ~2,000 contributors, and ~30,000 PRs. Steinberger describes running the OpenClaw Foundation as 'a company on hard mode,' improving but still insufficient bus factor, and building it as neutral 'Switzerland' inspired by Ghosti, pending American banking paperwork, to enable hiring full-time staff. Corporate contributors include Nvidia, Microsoft, Red Hat, Tencent, ByteDance, Slack, Salesforce, and others. Security is the core focus: 1,142 advisories (~16.6/day), 99 critical, 469 published, 60% closed—roughly double Linux kernel or curl volume. Many reports are AI-generated 'slop.' He critiques a university paper ('Agents of Chaos') and security companies for ignoring documented security recommendations, emphasizing the fundamental agentic risk applies to any powerful agent system. Steinberger joined OpenAI but clarifies they did not buy OpenClaw; he deliberately diversifies contributors to prevent takeover. In Q&A, he notes OpenAI's improving open-source stance, stresses OpenClaw must work with any model including local ones, and champions data ownership as a European value and 'the hacker way.' He describes his coding workflow: formerly ~10 concurrent agent sessions, now 5-6, as a workaround until token speeds improve. He rejects full 'dark factory' automation, comparing software development to a winding mountain path requiring iterative discovery. He identifies 'taste'—starting with not producing recognizable AI output—as the critical, hard-to-automate moat. Extending into personality, he explains how OpenClaw's WhatsApp integration evolved because Cloud Code's default personality felt too wordy for messaging contexts, leading him to iterate toward more human-like communication. He argues OpenClaw could not have emerged from an American company due to legal constraints around unsolved security problems. His future vision includes ubiquitous agents across every room in the home, with devices like iPads serving as contextual displays, and uppercase (work) and lowercase (personal) OpenClaw instances that can communicate with appropriate privacy boundaries. On prompt injection, he notes front-end models have improved at detecting untrusted content but acknowledges risks remain, especially with small local models lacking defenses—OpenClaw warns users about this. He reveals early work on 'dreaming,' a memory reconciliation process inspired by human sleep, and highlights OpenClaw's shift from spaghetti code to a modular extension/plugin architecture. For future skills, he emphasizes taste, system design, and the increasingly vital discipline of saying no—since any wild idea is just a prompt away, the real challenge is how multiple ideas compound and interconnect. He notes projects remain bottlenecked on big-picture syncing: agents thrown into a codebase see only local context, producing localized solutions, so the engineer's job is to provide hints about interplay and broader system considerations to yield maintainable results.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Project Growth and Statistics
sections.summary: Steinberger opens with OpenClaw's growth metrics: five months old, fastest-growing GitHub project, ~30,000 stars, approaching 2,000 contributors and 30,000 PRs, with velocity continuing. He notes running the OpenClaw Foundation is like a company on hard mode due to volunteer management.

sections.title: Management Challenges and Corporate Contributors
sections.summary: Discusses bus factor improvements, corporate contributors from Nvidia, Microsoft, Red Hat, Tencent, and ByteDance, with Chinese companies being the largest users.

sections.title: Addressing Security Advisories and Vulnerabilities
sections.summary: Details 1,142 security advisories (~16.6/day), 99 critical, 469 published, 60% closed—double Linux kernel and curl rates. Many are AI-generated slop. Examples include a CVSS-10 issue practically irrelevant due to unused features, North Korean Ghost Claw supply-chain attack, and Axios dependency issue. Nvidia helped with full-time security staff.

sections.title: Misinformation and Media Fearmongering
sections.summary: Critiques a university paper ('Agents of Chaos') and security companies for ignoring OpenClaw's security documentation to exaggerate risks, including running the agent in pseudo mode against recommendations. Emphasizes the core agentic risk model applies to any powerful agent system.

sections.title: The Burden of Open Source Maintenance
sections.summary: Describes the maintainer burden of reviewing AI-generated security reports, noting most lack fixes or include bad fixes. Mentions ffmpeg as another project facing similar issues. Begins clarifying that OpenAI did not buy OpenClaw.

sections.title: Foundation Independence and OpenAI Relationship
sections.summary: Steinberger explains the OpenClaw Foundation is being built as neutral 'Switzerland' inspired by Ghosti, pending banking paperwork, to hire full-time staff. In Q&A, he addresses the 'closed claw' joke, clarifies OpenAI did not buy OpenClaw, notes OpenAI's improving open-source stance (Codex, Symfony), and explains he deliberately diversifies contributors across Nvidia, Microsoft, Telegram, Salesforce, Slack, Tencent, ByteDance, and talks with Alibaba, Miniax, Kimi to prevent any single-company takeover.

sections.title: The Importance of Open and Local Models
sections.summary: Steinberger explains his motivation: data ownership as a European value, 'the hacker way' of bypassing corporate silos, and enabling cooler automation use cases that large companies cannot do. OpenClaw must work with any model, including local ones.

sections.title: Coding Workflow and Agent Interactions
sections.summary: Discusses his famous multi-agent workflow: formerly ~10 concurrent sessions, now 5-6 due to faster loops and fast mode, as a workaround until token speeds improve. Rejects full 'dark factory' automation, comparing software development to a winding mountain path requiring iterative discovery rather than a waterfall approach.

sections.title: Defining 'Taste' in AI Development
sections.summary: Defines taste starting at the lowest level: output that doesn't 'stink like AI'—recognizable AI writing style, personality, and UI patterns (purple gradients, colored borders). Taste is a 'smell' you instinctively identify. As more software becomes automatable, taste and attention to detail become the differentiating moat.

sections.title: Developing Personality for AI Agents
sections.summary: Steinberger and Swix discuss how OpenClaw's personality emerged through iteration. When Steinberger connected OpenClaw to WhatsApp via a relay, the default Cloud Code personality felt too wordy and formal for messaging. He iterated toward more human-like text, telling the agent to 'write more like a human.' Swix notes this 'madness with a touch of science fiction' approach could not have emerged from an American company due to legal constraints around unsolved security problems.

sections.title: Future Vision: Ubiquitous Agents and Smart Homes
sections.summary: Steinberger envisions talking to his agent from any room in his home, Star Trek-style, with iPads serving as contextual displays the agent can project onto based on location awareness. He imagines ubiquitous agents with an uppercase (work) OpenClaw and lowercase (personal) OpenClaw that can communicate with appropriate privacy boundaries. Swix notes Karpathy and Maran Dre run OpenClaw for their homes, and that smart device security weaknesses ironically enable OpenClaw to control them.

sections.title: Addressing Prompt Injection Risks
sections.summary: Steinberger says front-end models are now quite good at detecting untrusted content from websites and emails, making prompt injection no longer the biggest problem for well-configured systems. However, small local models (~20B parameters) lack training defenses, creating real risk when combined with web browsers or email. OpenClaw warns users about small models; Steinberger clarifies this isn't hating local models but steering users away from unsafe configurations. Mentions Simon Willison's dual LLM approach and a trust/reputation system for privileged access.

sections.title: Future Vision: Implementing 'Dreaming' and Modularity
sections.summary: Steinberger reveals early work on 'dreaming'—a memory reconciliation process where agents review session logs, convert local memories to long-term storage, and drop others, analogous to human sleep. The Anthropic source code leak confirmed they are also working on this. He highlights OpenClaw's evolution from spaghetti code to a modular extension/plugin architecture, enabling users to add memory, wikis, dreaming, or custom features without submitting PRs, similar to Linux's installable components.

sections.title: Life as a Maintainer and Future Skills
sections.summary: Steinberger describes his daily role shifting toward talking and steering people, sharing lessons learned at OpenClaw with OpenAI to prevent repeated mistakes, and enabling companies to build custom OpenClaw configurations. For future engineer skills, he emphasizes taste, system design, and the discipline of saying no—any wild idea is just a prompt away, but the compounding of multiple ideas and their interconnections is the real problem. He notes projects remain bottlenecked on big-picture syncing: agents thrown into a codebase see only local context and produce localized solutions, so the engineer's job is to provide hints about broader interplay and system considerations to yield maintainable systems. Swyx closes by thanking Steinberger for maintaining 'one of the most important software of all time.'
